title: เคลิ้ม · Klə́əm (Swooning)
about: A rock ballad about loving someone you know is bad for you. One look into their eyes and your heart 'floats away' again. Useful for: the casual 'you' (təə), dtɛ̀ɛ gɔ̂ɔ (but still), duang (the classifier for hearts) and feelings vocabulary.

lines.r: rúu dii təə nâ jai ráai
lines.th: รู้ดีเธอน่ะใจร้าย
lines.en: I know full well you're heartless
lines.note: rúu dii = know very well. nâ is a soft spoken particle that marks the topic: 'you, you're heartless'. Subject 'I' is dropped, as in most songs and casual speech.

lines.r: dtɛ̀ɛ gɔ̂ɔ rák təə mâi rúu tammai
lines.th: แต่ก็รักเธอไม่รู้ทำไม
lines.en: but I still love you, I don't know why
lines.note: dtɛ̀ɛ gɔ̂ɔ = but still (the same gɔ̂ɔ as tʉ̌ng … gɔ̂ɔ). mâi rúu tammai = 'don't know why', very common in casual speech.

lines.r: piang sòp dtaa təə, jai duang dəəm klə́əm lɔɔi bpai
lines.th: เพียงสบตาเธอ ใจดวงเดิม เคลิ้มลอยไป
lines.en: just meeting your eyes, my same old heart drifts off in a daze
lines.note: The hook. piang = just, only. sòp dtaa = to meet someone's eyes. duang is the classifier for hearts (also sun, moon, stars). dəəm = the same as before. klə́əm = dreamy, swooning, half-asleep. lɔɔi bpai = float away.

lines.r: hǔa jai duang níi mâi làap jam
lines.th: หัวใจดวงนี้ไม่หลาบจำ
lines.en: this heart never learns its lesson
lines.note: noun + classifier + níi again: hǔa jai duang níi = this heart. làap jam = to learn your lesson (after something bad).

lines.th: หัวใจนี่มันงมงาย
lines.en: this heart of mine is so gullible
lines.note: nîi man … = casual way to complain about something, like 'this thing, it's …'. man = it (also used casually for animals and annoying things). ngom-ngaai = blindly believing, gullible.

lines.r: jəə təə túk tii gɔ̂ɔ lǒng taang bpai
lines.th: เจอเธอทุกทีก็หลงทางไป
lines.en: every time I see you, I lose my way
lines.note: túk tii = every time (casual for túk kráng). lǒng taang = to get lost; here, to lose yourself.

words: can't help but, still keep on
ทำร้ายตัวเอง
cursed, darned (about something that keeps causing trouble)
to come back, go back (in time)
notes: Songs use təə (you) and chán (I) for lovers. In speech, təə is used between partners or close friends, mostly by women; many people just use names or kun.
Song lyrics drop subjects even more than speech does: 'rák təə mâi rúu tammai' (I love you, I don't know why). Work out who is doing what from context.
The singer talks about hǔa jai (the heart) as if it were a separate stubborn person: it doesn't listen, it doesn't learn, it hurts itself. Thai songs do this a lot.
ไซร้ (sái), near the end of the song, is an old-fashioned poetic word for emphasis. You'll see it in songs, but don't use it when you speak.
